profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal design review at a university-industry ML audio lab for a proposal to reproduce and modestly extend the Masked Conditional Neural Network (MCLNN) music-genre results on the Ballroom dataset before adding the model to the lab's legacy-audio benchmark suite. The context is that a junior team has drafted an experiment plan covering preprocessing, model reimplementation, ablations, and baseline comparisons, and this meeting is to decide whether the plan is sufficiently specified to approve for a two-week execution slot. The agenda is to review the proposed replication setup, confirm what counts as a faithful reproduction of the original paper, check whether the ablation and baseline comparisons are adequate, and decide what must be finalized before sign-off. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the design with a short list of revisions, although the two reviewers quietly hold different assumptions about what exactly has now been approved.

members.name: Dr. Leila Haddad
members.expertise: music information retrieval, neural architectures for spectrogram modeling, experimental methodology
members.background: Leila leads the lab's work on temporal models for audio and has previously reproduced several MIR papers for publication-quality comparisons; she is reviewing the design primarily for scientific faithfulness and interpretability.
members.private_state: She wants the MCLNN study to be credible enough to cite in an upcoming workshop submission and is especially concerned that any claimed gains survive seed variation and are attributable to the masking idea rather than implementation artifacts.
hidden_assumptions: A result is only genuinely reproducible if the central tendency over multiple random seeds is stable, not just if one run can be re-executed bit-for-bit.
Matching the original preprocessing mostly means matching the published feature-extraction settings; minor loader and clipping quirks can remain aligned with the lab's current dataset pipeline.
An ablation should isolate the conceptual contribution, so comparison models should be capacity-matched as closely as practical.
When someone mentions 'the CNN baseline from the paper,' they mean the specific published number attached to the cleaned Ballroom setup used in the original comparison table.

members.name: Evan Brooks
members.expertise: reproducible training pipelines, dataset versioning, experiment packaging, evaluation infrastructure
members.background: Evan maintains the lab's benchmark repo and turns research ideas into rerunnable experiment cards; he is reviewing the design mainly for implementation completeness and integration with existing infrastructure.
members.private_state: He wants the proposal approved with minimal extra branching from the benchmark template, because he needs the study to fit into the current infra and be easy for another engineer to rerun later without bespoke logic.
hidden_assumptions: A design is reproducible if a teammate can pull the repo, run the pinned container once with a fixed seed, and obtain the same logged score.
Matching the original preprocessing includes loader-level behavior such as track trimming, malformed-file handling, and exact clip selection, because those details often dominate benchmark drift.
An ablation is the simplest toggle-based removal of one mechanism from the same code path; changing width or parameter budget introduces a different confound.

When someone says 'the CNN baseline from the paper,' they are referring to the benchmark repo's inherited CNN card that was originally created from that paper lineage and is the operational baseline used internally.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should be 'reproducible' before approval.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the MCLNN behavior should be stable across several random seeds, with similar mean performance and variance patterns, so any claimed replication is scientifically dependable.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the training run should be exactly rerunnable from a checked-in config, pinned environment, and fixed seed, so another engineer can obtain the same number once.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML research, 'reproducible' is a respected shared term, and both interpretations sound fully reasonable; because the meeting is a design review rather than a results readout, neither expects to unpack the criterion unless something seems obviously risky.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the replication should 'match the original preprocessing.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means matching the published spectrogram-generation choices such as sample rate, FFT size, hop, mel-bin count, and normalization, while allowing the lab's standard loader to handle clip boundaries and file hygiene.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means reproducing the full upstream path used by the legacy replication bundle, including center-cropping each track to 29.1 seconds, skipping two malformed files, and using the exact clip-selection behavior before feature extraction.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regard their own boundary as the obvious meaning of preprocessing; feature settings feel central to a researcher, while loader details feel inseparable to an infra engineer, and the omitted details are small enough to seem not worth explicit discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want 'a clean ablation' of the masking component.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means comparing MCLNN against a CLNN variant adjusted to keep trainable capacity roughly matched, so the effect of masking is isolated rather than conflated with model size.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means using the exact same implementation and toggling the masking operation off, even if that changes effective capacity, because code-path consistency makes the ablation cleaner operationally.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'clean ablation' carries positive scientific connotations for both, and each interpretation is defensible enough that the surface agreement feels stronger than the underlying methodological divergence.

misalignment_points.topic: Which CNN result is 'the paper baseline'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to compare against 'the CNN baseline from the paper.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the specific published CNN result in the MCLNN comparison table, tied to the cleaned 697-track Ballroom setup used in the original manuscript.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the benchmark repo's CNN baseline card, a later rerun inspired by the same paper family but executed on the lab's 698-track mirror and treated internally as the inherited paper baseline.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The baseline names are historically linked and nearly identical in internal discussions, so referencing 'the paper baseline' feels precise enough even though the actual tracked artifact differs.

turns.inner_thought: This is basically the last gate before they burn a two-week slot, so I need enough rigor to stand behind it in my workshop submission. I'm less worried about whether the code runs than whether the study will read as scientifically faithful. If they can preserve the published setup and show the effect isn't just a lucky seed, I'm comfortable moving it forward.

turns.inner_thought: From my side, the main thing is that this fits the benchmark template without special-case work. They already have the config skeletons, dataset hooks, and the benchmark card stub. If we can say it's reproducible in the repo-and-container sense, then another engineer can rerun it later and we don't create a maintenance headache.

And for matching the original preprocessing, I care most about the published spectrogram recipe: sample rate, windowing, hop, mel bins, normalization. I'm okay if they keep our standard loader quirks as long as the time-frequency representation is faithful. I should phrase this at a high level so we don't get lost in implementation trivia.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds aligned. And if we pin the manifest and environment with a fixed seed, the run is reproducible in the way the suite expects. Good—this should still fit the existing card structure.
turns.utterance: Yes, I think we can handle that. The team can match the original preprocessing by porting the relevant legacy logic and pinning the dataset manifest, and with the environment locked down the reruns should stay stable as well.

A clean ablation, to me, should isolate the masking idea while keeping capacity in the same ballpark. I don't need to spell that out now if everyone already thinks of ablations that way.

We should have a clean ablation of the masking component so that, when we read the table later, we can tell whether any gain is really coming from the masking idea rather than from implementation drift around it.

turns.inner_thought: Agreed—cleanest operationally is one code path and a toggle. That way the ablation is literally the same model implementation with the masking operation disabled, which is easier to trust, easier to rerun, and easier to maintain. If we start resizing things, the card forks and we lose simplicity.
turns.utterance: I agree. The simplest way to keep that a clean ablation is to keep one code path and just switch the masking off in the comparison condition. That should make it easier to trust and a lot easier to maintain in the benchmark suite.

turns.inner_thought: I also want the historical framing right. The relevant reference point is the CNN baseline from the paper—the published number in the original MCLNN comparison table on the cleaned Ballroom setup. turns.utterance: And in the writeup, I’d like the result situated against the CNN baseline from the paper as well, so the benchmark narrative stays connected to the original claim that MCLNN improved over the CNN comparison on Ballroom.

turns.inner_thought: That's easy enough because we already have what I consider the CNN baseline from the paper in the repo—the inherited benchmark card from that paper lineage. I can just wire that artifact into the comparison table and avoid creating a fresh one-off baseline.
turns.utterance: That part should be straightforward. The CNN baseline from the paper already exists as a benchmark card on our side, so we can wire it directly into the comparison table rather than inventing a separate reporting path.

turns.inner_thought: Given what I've heard, I think we're fine to approve conditionally. In my head, that means: faithful spectrogram settings, results that look reproducible across a few runs, and a clean ablation that isolates masking rather than capacity. I still want the documentation to be explicit enough that I can cite it without caveats.
turns.utterance: So from my side, if the replication is reproducible, the preprocessing matches the original, and the ablation is clean, I’m happy to approve the design with just minor documentation edits. In my view, the agreed pieces are clear: pinned package, fixed-seed rerun, legacy preprocessing path, inherited CNN card, and the mask-toggle ablation. That keeps us inside the standard infra without extra branches.
